extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, judges, agency counsel, and rulemaking practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrinal/practical guidance on an agency’s obligation under the APA and related authorities to consider and (when appropriate) reply to public comments in notice-and-comment and interim-final rulemaking. The page analyzes legal foundations, policy tradeoffs, scope, exceptions, and collateral applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to respond to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: "An agency must consider and respond to significant comments received during the period for public comment." (Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass’n dictum)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a procedural duty under the APA; adopted as an expected step in rulemaking. The duty operationalizes § 553(c)’s requirement to 'consider' comments by requiring responses to material/significant ones. Courts and agencies generally accept this as a normal component of rule development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / materiality threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant comments are those that are 'material' or 'significant' enough to require a response — often characterized by Portland Cement’s "step over a threshold requirement of materiality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts use a materiality threshold to limit the scope of the duty to respond. The standard is vague and fact-specific but aims to avoid obligating agencies to reply to trivial remarks. Ambiguity in the standard is tolerable given need for judicial flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part formulation of 'significant' comments (relevance + change-if-adopted)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common case-law formulation: significant comments are (1) relevant and (2) would require a change in the rule if adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevancy is straightforward; 'would require a change' captures comments pointing out mistakes or cogent criticisms. Courts must assess whether the neglected comment was persuasive enough to deserve a response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions — obscure, speculative, or buried comments need not be answered
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies do not need to respond to comments that are obscurely stated, purely speculative, or buried inconspicuously in a lengthy advocacy document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/cases: Northside Sanitary Landfill (forfeiture where commenter failed to put EPA on notice), Pub. Citizen v. FAA (speculative), CTS Corp. v. EPA (buried). These categories allow agencies to focus on material submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment must be relevant to the rule for the duty to respond to attach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have rejected the need to answer comments irrelevant to the rule's subject or that do not bear on the agency’s decisionmaking factors (e.g., Am. Mining Cong. v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must respond to substantial arguments in testimony and comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency’s concise explanatory statement must contain: '(1) the agency’s reasons for adopting the rule, including the agency’s reasons for not accepting substantial arguments made in testimony and comments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should address substantial objections, explain why they are rejected, and include reasons in the rule’s statement of basis and purpose; perfunctory recitals are insufficient (see La. Fed. Land Bank).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to respond to proposed alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should respond to alternative courses of action that commenters actually proposed during the notice-and-comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (e.g., Deacon) emphasize that responses to proposed alternatives facilitate judicial review, accountability, and higher-quality decisionmaking. Responses should explain why alternatives were accepted or rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfunctory recitals are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere recital that the agency 'considered' comments or 'noted' them without analysis will not satisfy the duty to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will invalidate final rules where the agency merely 'noted' authorities or comments without analyzing their arguments (e.g., La. Fed. Land Bank Ass’n v. Farm Credit Admin.). Agencies must provide meaningful explanation for ignoring or rejecting significant points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing the materiality inquiry (could vs reasonably could have influenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether materiality should be framed as whether the comment 'might' have changed the agency’s mind (low bar) or whether the agency could reasonably have failed to take account of the comment (better framing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid too-low standards that render every minor comment 'material'; asking whether the agency could reasonably have failed to account for the comment is a more administrable test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency consideration may be satisfied even if no regulatory change is made
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency can satisfy the duty by considering comments and explaining its position even if it ultimately makes no changes to the proposed rule (Little Sisters majority view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that the rule remained unchanged does not by itself prove the agency failed to consider comments; the record must show actual consideration and reasoned responses where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim-final rulemaking and post-promulgation comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies issue interim final rules with a 'good cause' finding (forgoing pre-promulgation notice-and-comment), they typically invite post-promulgation comments and should respond to significant adverse comments in a replacement rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS recommends that invitations to post-promulgation comment state the agency will respond to significant comments. Courts vary on whether post-promulgation procedures cure an initial good-cause error; some require open-minded consideration of comments or changes in the replacement rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exemption requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: APA § 553 allows agencies to dispense with notice-and-comment if procedure would be 'impracticable,' 'unnecessary,' or 'contrary to the public interest,' but the agency must make an explicit 'good cause' finding explaining why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-cause findings are subject to judicial review; misuse can lead to vacatur of interim rules unless remedied through meaningful post-promulgation consideration and response to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-mindedness test (post-promulgation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts have held that, to validate a replacement rule after interim final rulemaking, the agency must have considered post-promulgation comments 'with a mind that is open to persuasion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is contested. The Supreme Court in Little Sisters criticized imposing such an open-mindedness requirement as lacking textual support, but lower courts and commentators still discuss it as a measure of adequate post-promulgation consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue-exhaustion for judicial review of rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner generally must have raised an issue during the notice-and-comment period to preserve it for judicial review (issue-exhaustion doctrines and ACUS Statement #19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are exceptions and some circuit variation (key-assumption exception, etc.). Practitioners should timely present objections with reasonable specificity to avoid forfeiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason-giving fosters accountability and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason-giving requirements compel agencies to articulate justifications for their actions, enabling affected interests to evaluate and participate in a dialogue about official policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly defenses (Weinberg, Mashaw) emphasize epistemic and legitimating values: better-informed decisions, public trust, and the ability of stakeholders to assess agency reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs: ossification and strategic flooding
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to respond can slow rulemaking (ossification) and be exploited by well-funded interest groups that inundate agencies with comments for strategic advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and policymakers must weigh procedural benefits against administrative burdens; the comment process itself screens for important issues but is not costless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial enforcement should avoid substituting judges’ policy judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts enforcing the duty must be cautious not to derail necessary regulatory actions by giving undue weight to minor or ambiguously raised objections (concern illustrated by Ohio v. EPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial unfamiliarity with technical subjects and judges’ own biases can skew application of the duty; enforcement should respect agency expertise and not over-police modest defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of mass, computer-generated, and identical comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are not required to ensure that a person reads each identical or nearly identical comment; they may use sorting software and other tools to manage large volumes (ACUS Recommendations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS Recommendation 2011-1 and 2021-1 address e-rulemaking and managing mass/falsely attributed comments; agencies may rely on sampling, categorization, and automation to identify material issues among floods of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/regulatory contexts with explicit response duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Some statutes (e.g., Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, Regulatory Flexibility Act) already require agencies to respond to certain comments or to discuss specific considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statute-specific duties informed and anticipated the broader adoption of a duty-to-respond norm under the APA; agencies should be mindful of these heightened obligations in specialized proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: duty does not extend to every comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to respond is not limitless; commentators who fail to state objections with reasonable specificity or who raise irrelevant issues may forfeit the right to have those matters considered on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show courts policing adequacy of notice to the agency (e.g., Northside) and rejecting claims based on comments that leave the agency guessing about the grievance (Oakbrook/Hewitt contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concise explanatory statement in rulemaking records
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules should include a concise explanatory statement describing the agency’s reasons for adopting the rule and for not accepting substantial arguments in testimony and comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements are central to satisfying the APA’s reason-giving and consideration obligations and provide the basis for judicial review of whether the agency responded adequately to material comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay with procedural fairness and standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking procedure (including comment-response duties) is designed to serve collective public goals (accuracy, accountability) rather than to guarantee individualized fairness; its procedural errors may or may not create plaintiff-specific injuries relevant to standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish between procedure that advances collective goals and individual due-process rights; procedural defects in rulemaking are analyzed in light of their practical consequences for plaintiffs (e.g., Lujan, Earth Island analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility of judicial standards—no talismanic words
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review standards (like 'significant,' 'substantial evidence') cannot assure certainty of application; courts need flexibility to apply undefined but functional terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levin cites Universal Camera/Frankfurter: some indeterminacy is inherent, and courts must exercise judgment rather than rely on fixed textual formulas when reviewing agencies’ responses to comments.
